blocks.text: **Keep spoken categories separate from written symbols.** Identifying a letter is not the same task as identifying a phoneme.
A letter can contribute to different pronunciations, and a phoneme can be represented by different spellings.
**An unfamiliar spelling cannot always be decoded correctly from its letters alone.** Deep orthographies create more exceptions that readers must learn through experience.
COLONEL and PARADIGM make the problem concrete. Applying common letter–sound patterns can produce a plausible-looking pronunciation that is wrong for the actual word.
children: In shallower writing systems, such as Finnish and Korean, spelling–sound correspondences are more predictable. The comparison concerns the writing system, not the intelligence or ability of its readers.

blocks.text: **Consistent correspondences make decoding easier to generalize.** Finnish readers can apply what they learn about letters to unfamiliar written forms.
Doubled letters represent a meaningful length distinction. A doubled consonant is geminated, and a doubled vowel is long.
children: This regularity helps Finnish children learn decoding quickly. Decoding means generating a pronunciation from a written form, whether or not its meaning is familiar.

blocks.text: **A made-up word separates decoding from remembering a familiar word.** The lower English performance is consistent with greater orthographic depth.

The comparison involves Grade 1 children learning different alphabetic writing systems. Children learning many other languages produce plausible pseudoword pronunciations more successfully than English learners.
children: English's less predictable correspondences help explain why decoding develops more slowly. This task does not measure the child's entire language ability.

blocks.text: **The organization of Hangul supports more than consistent pronunciation.** Similar sound categories can also be visibly related in their written symbols.
The letters are arranged into syllable blocks with initial, medial and sometimes final positions. Those positions are not three unrelated pictures of whole words.
children: The velar consonant forms share the basic angular ㄱ shape. Additional strokes or doubling distinguish related consonants.

blocks.text: **Reading a novel letter sequence reveals knowledge beyond memorized words.** Familiar spelling patterns support pronunciation of new combinations.
Success cannot depend on retrieving a stored pronunciation for each particular item. The reader is using knowledge that generalizes across words.
children: The demonstration establishes generalization. By itself, it does not decide whether that knowledge consists of categorical rules or learned statistical patterns.

blocks.text: **Fast nonword naming is evidence that decoding is a normal part of skilled reading.** It does not by itself prove that a separate rule system performs the task.

Participants read the items aloud, and naming time measures how quickly a pronunciation becomes available. The small difference shows that unfamiliarity does not make pronunciation an entirely slow, deliberate process.
children: Both rules and statistical generalization might produce efficient decoding. The speed result constrains a theory without selecting one architecture on its own.

blocks.text: **Generalization can be graded rather than all-or-none.** Ambiguous pseudowords reveal competing pronunciation possibilities.
A response reflects the spelling–sound patterns available from previously learned words. Different familiar patterns can favor different responses to the same novel form.
**Accepting both /strɛd/ and /strid/ is information about the knowledge being generalized.** A model must explain the alternatives, not merely choose one output and ignore the other.
Testing novel items reveals what a reader has generalized, because the particular word cannot simply have been memorized.
children: The challenge for a categorical rule account is to explain why multiple outputs seem acceptable. A statistical account can represent differing support for alternative pronunciations.

blocks.text: **A word's difficulty depends partly on how its spelling neighbors are pronounced.** The issue is not simply whether the reader knows the letters.
A strict regular–irregular division is less clear when a spelling neighborhood contains several pronunciations. ROLL, POLL and TOLL support one pattern, while DOLL differs.
children: COOK, TOOK and BOOK likewise contrast with SPOOK. These neighborhoods motivate asking how much support a pronunciation has from similar words.

blocks.text: **General decoding explains part of reading, but familiar-word knowledge also needs an account.** The two sources of information are conceptually distinguishable even before deciding how they are implemented.
**Lexical information** concerns knowledge of particular words. A complete account must explain how experience with a specific word contributes alongside general spelling patterns.
**Letter recognition can depend on the word surrounding the letter.** Feedback supplies a mechanism by which whole-word knowledge influences perception.
Activated word candidates send feedback to their constituent letters. A letter supported by a plausible word receives additional activation even when its local visual evidence is unclear.
children: Competing candidates do not remain equally active. Their activation changes as the network settles on an interpretation.

blocks.text: **Recognizing a word and recognizing its letters can support one another.** Top-down feedback is the word-to-letter part of that interaction.
This makes recognition interactive. Information does not flow only from isolated features upward to a finished word.
children: The mechanism helps explain why an ambiguous letter can become easier to recognize when it appears in a familiar word context.

blocks.text: **Familiarity with a particular word contributes to reading speed.** Knowing general spelling patterns does not remove the benefit of repeated encounters with that word.
Lexicality compares whether the item is a word. Frequency compares how often a particular word has been encountered.
children: The English Lexicon Project data show that the frequency effect occurs across many observations, rather than depending on a few unusually easy examples.

blocks.text: **The frequency effect is not adequately explained by saying that frequent words are merely shorter.** Its contribution survives statistical control of other properties.
The analysis uses about 3,000 words read by young and older adults. Frequency still contributes when other predictors are considered.
children: This makes a simple length-confound explanation less plausible. It does not turn an observational predictor into an experimentally isolated cause.

blocks.text: **Experience matters especially when pronunciation conflicts with the usual spelling pattern.** Frequent exposure reduces the disadvantage of exception words.
Naming latency is the time needed to begin saying the word. Higher values mean slower responses.
children: An interaction means the effect of one factor depends on the other. The regularity cost is not a fixed amount added equally to high- and low-frequency words.

blocks.text: **Two routes can explain why regularity matters most for unfamiliar words.** Fast lexical processing protects familiar exceptions from competing sublexical output.
For a high-frequency word, lexical information becomes available quickly enough to reduce the influence of the decoding output.
children: For a low-frequency exception, the lexical response is less efficient and the regularized decoding output can interfere. Nonwords depend on decoding because they lack a stored whole-word entry.

blocks.text: **Preserved word reading does not guarantee preserved decoding.** A patient can draw on learned word information while performing poorly on novel letter sequences.

Cacciopo van Vliet and colleagues compare real-word reading with several nonword tasks. The patients can often recognize and pronounce known words while struggling to generate a plausible pronunciation for an unfamiliar spelling.
children: The selective difficulty suggests that familiar-word success and novel-form decoding do not rely on every process to the same degree.

blocks.text: **Surface dyslexia exposes the cost of relying on typical correspondences when a word is exceptional.** The errors are systematic rather than arbitrary failures to see the letters.
DEAF pronounced like “deef” and SHOE pronounced like “show” illustrate regularization. The response is related to the spelling, but it is not the target word's learned pronunciation.
children: Relatively good regular-word and nonword reading shows that generating pronunciation from spelling can remain useful despite difficulty with exceptions.

blocks.text: **Opposite patient patterns support separable contributions to reading.** They are stronger evidence than a single group doing worse on one difficult task.

The first pattern shows that unfamiliar decoding can be difficult despite relatively preserved familiar-word reading. The second shows that exception reading can be difficult despite relatively preserved pseudoword reading.
children: Together, the patterns are harder to explain by saying that one task is simply harder for everyone.

blocks.text: **The strength of a double dissociation comes from the reversal across cases.** The interpretation must explain both directions of impairment.
The reversal suggests that the tasks depend differently on underlying processes. For reading, pseudowords and exception words place different demands on the system.
children: The evidence still requires a theory of what those underlying processes are. It does not uniquely identify a particular set of boxes in a model.

blocks.text: **The model turns an observed dissociation into a claim about damaged processing components.** Each proposed lesion must produce the corresponding pattern of spared and impaired performance.
Damage to conversion particularly affects nonwords because there is no familiar whole-word pronunciation to retrieve.
children: Damage to input or output word representations, called logogens in this account, or their connections makes exceptions vulnerable because general decoding supplies the wrong pronunciation.

blocks.text: **A patient's error type matters as well as overall accuracy.** Lexical-looking errors challenge the idea that the remaining reading process is wholly independent of word knowledge.
The example “incense” read as “increase” is a real-word response. A simple letter–sound mistake could instead produce a nonword, so the actual response raises a question about whole-word influence.
children: Possible responses are to allow a more complicated combination of routes or to revise the supposedly nonlexical process itself. The observation motivates refinement rather than settling the issue alone.

blocks.text: **The two-route proposal connects several reading findings to a common processing account.** Its success depends on explaining the full pattern, not only nonword reading.
A model must explain fast pseudoword reading, faster familiar-word reading, frequency effects, regularity effects and their interaction.
children: It must also explain why pseudoword and exception-word reading can be differently impaired after brain injury. These observations motivate the architecture but do not uniquely prove it.

blocks.text: **The DRC does not treat every connection as the same kind of computation.** Word-form activation and rule-based conversion are separate mechanisms.
The lexical portion includes orthographic and phonological lexicons, representing written and spoken word forms. These representations are distinguished from meanings.
children: The implementation described here does not implement semantics. The GPC rule system also has processing assumptions different from those of the interactive lexical network.

blocks.text: **Encapsulation does not mean that the routes never affect the same response.** They remain separate internally but meet at the phoneme output.
The GPC and lexical routes do not interact throughout their internal computations. They converge in the phoneme response buffer.
children: If the routes favor different phonemes, they can compete at that shared output. An exception word can therefore receive a correct lexical pronunciation and an incompatible regularized pronunciation.

blocks.text: **A rule list is incomplete without a procedure for resolving overlapping rules.** Both the mapping and its conditions of application matter.
A model also needs a way to decide which applicable rule takes priority. A larger-unit rule can supersede rules for its individual letters.
children: Context-sensitive rules restrict a pronunciation to specified surrounding letters or positions. This makes the procedure more than a simple lookup of one sound per letter.

blocks.text: **Using statistics to select a rule differs from representing graded statistics while reading.** The two approaches can make different predictions for ambiguous spellings.
The possible pronunciations of OUGH have more divided statistical support than those of EIGH. A rule can still operate categorically for both spellings.
children: A probabilistic account instead allows alternatives to receive different strengths of support. The distinction concerns processing, not whether the model designer ever consulted frequency information.

blocks.text: **A cognitively useful model should reproduce the relevant failures.** Maximizing pronunciation accuracy is not the only goal.
A regularizing route helps account for errors in surface dyslexia and for slow naming of low-frequency exception words.
children: The theory therefore claims that people's sublexical computation is constrained, rather than assuming that the best possible spelling algorithm is the correct cognitive model.

blocks.text: **A modular account predicts restricted access to information.** The GPC route may produce an inappropriate response even when another part of the system has word-specific knowledge.
This resembles a modular parsing proposal in which an early syntactic process follows structural principles without immediately using world knowledge.
children: Pseudoword naming exposes the conversion procedure because a familiar lexical entry is unavailable. Regularization errors expose it when conversion favors the wrong pronunciation.

blocks.text: **A broad list of successful simulations is informative, but the conditions of each success also matter.** Model evaluation includes both coverage and the assumptions used to obtain it.
Accounting for several effects with one architecture is stronger than fitting a single result. It also requires examining which assumptions stay fixed and which are changed between tasks.
children: The model's research strategy places strong weight on human behavioral evidence as a constraint on architecture.

blocks.text: **Fitting lexical decision requires an account of the decision itself.** Recognition activity does not automatically specify when to say yes or no.
A “yes” response can depend on a strongly activated single word or on total activity across the orthographic lexicon. A “no” response occurs if the criteria are not met by a deadline.
children: The implementation also changes inhibition and uses time-dependent thresholds. These choices help obtain a fit, but they add assumptions beyond the basic two-route diagram.

blocks.text: **Modularity is a claim about how components operate and communicate.** It is more specific than drawing two arrows in a model.
The GPC system takes letters as input and sends phoneme activation toward the response system. This is **domain specificity** in the account.
children: The absence of lexical feedback into the GPC system is **informational encapsulation**. Having two pathways alone would not establish those stronger restrictions.

blocks.text: **An emergentist account asks how experience creates useful reading behavior.** Regularity can arise from learning across words rather than from a separate rule mechanism.
Seidenberg and McClelland trained an associative network to map spelling onto pronunciation. The modeled spelling-to-sound pathway used one learned mapping for different kinds of words.
children: Reading skill emerges from learning rather than being specified entirely as a hand-built list of rules and lexical entries.

blocks.text: **Word-specific knowledge and generalization can coexist in the same learned system.** They do not have to be implemented as a dictionary and a separate symbolic rule list.
The same learning mechanism can capture both patterns shared by many words and information specific to a familiar word.
children: The research strategy asks whether domain-general learning can explain reading. This contrasts with choosing separate adult processing components primarily from neuropsychological dissociations.

blocks.text: **Consistency supplies support from other words, while frequency strengthens experience with the particular word.** Their joint influence explains why infrequent exceptions are especially difficult.
An exception conflicts with those patterns, so learning its particular mapping is especially important. Frequent exposure strengthens that word-specific mapping.
children: A low-frequency exception has both weak item-specific learning and poor support from the dominant pattern. This combination creates a larger disadvantage than either factor alone.

blocks.text: **Spelling–sound support varies in degree.** A statistical description captures differences that a simple regular-versus-irregular label can hide.
LATE and DUST illustrate consistent patterns. GAVE and MINT have many friends but also enemies such as HAVE and PINT.
children: DOWN versus KNOWN and POUR versus SOUR illustrate ambiguity. An exception such as PINT has relatively little support compared with its competing neighborhood.

blocks.text: **Novel pronunciation can result from applying learned statistical structure.** Nonword reading therefore does not automatically establish a separate symbolic route.
No stored entry for the particular nonword is required. The same learned correspondences that support consistent words can support a new combination.
children: This is a proposed mechanism for decoding without a separate GPC rule module.

blocks.text: **A failed simulation does not identify its own cause.** The failure must be traced to the architecture, learning assumptions, representations or other implementation choices.
One possibility is that a single associative mechanism cannot explain the task. Another is that the chosen representations fail to capture the similarities needed for generalization.
children: Improving the implementation while retaining the theoretical mechanism helps distinguish these possibilities.

blocks.text: **Changing the representation can improve decoding without adding a symbolic rule system.** That distinction matters when evaluating the original theoretical claim.
Plaut and colleagues improved the phonological representations and obtained better nonword performance. This supports a representational explanation for at least part of the earlier failure.
children: Behavioral relations between phonological processing and decoding also make phonology a relevant target for explanation.

blocks.text: **The same representational weakness can have unequal effects on words and nonwords.** Familiarity can partly compensate where new-item generalization cannot.
A familiar word can retain support from its own training history. A nonword lacks that item-specific experience and depends more heavily on generalization.
children: This produces a reason for unfamiliar forms to be especially vulnerable to poor representations without requiring a dedicated nonword mechanism.

blocks.text: **A selective-looking reading deficit can emerge from degraded shared representations.** Nonwords are especially dependent on reliable generalization.
The manipulation produced poorer nonword decoding and relative sparing of word recognition. It also linked the severity of the phonological deficit to the degree of decoding difficulty.
children: The model therefore connects a reading pattern to the quality of a more general phonological system.

blocks.text: **The model links exception reading to semantic processing.** A reading dissociation can reflect unequal dependence on broader language systems.
An exception has weak support from typical spelling–sound regularities. Meaning-related support can help produce its learned pronunciation.
children: Reducing that support creates a surface-dyslexia-like pattern without defining a separate exception-word list as the sole explanation.

blocks.text: **Multiple pathways do not necessarily imply modular routes.** Their learning rules, information types and interactions distinguish the accounts.
Spelling-to-sound learning develops in the presence of meaning-related support. The contribution of one pathway therefore affects what another pathway learns.
children: This allows graded impairments. Phonological dyslexics can make some exception errors, and surface dyslexics can make some nonword errors.

blocks.text: **The triangle account predicts that exception reading should vary with semantic ability.** The patient data broadly follow that relationship.
The model and patient panels show comparable overall relationships, although individual patients vary. This supports an association between meaning and exceptional pronunciation.
children: The finding is informative because it links a reading weakness to a broader semantic measure rather than describing only a reading-task dissociation.

blocks.text: **An outlier and a clean dissociation are not automatically the same thing.** The strength and reliability of the apparent exception matter.
Woollams and colleagues interpret such observations in relation to the full distribution rather than treating each outlier as an automatic refutation.
children: The scientific issue is whether the unusual cases show a stable separate pattern or arise within a noisy overall association.

blocks.text: **Repeated observations help test whether an apparent dissociation persists.** A one-time exceptional score is less compelling if the patient's later trajectory follows the general relation.
In most cases, declining semantic ability accompanies declining exception-word reading. Some initially unusual observations move closer to the broader relation on retesting.
children: This strengthens the association while leaving room for variability between individuals.

blocks.text: **A flexible model can closely reproduce observed data.** Evaluating the explanation also requires asking how the matching simulation was selected.
This produced an excellent fit to the patient scores. The selection procedure is part of how that fit was achieved.
children: The fit should be distinguished from predicting each patient's pattern before choosing among many possible parameter combinations.

blocks.text: **Goodness of fit is only one part of model evaluation.** A model should explain why the pattern occurs, not only contain a setting that resembles it.
The question is not whether close agreement is bad in itself. It is whether the account predicts the relation with principled assumptions or accommodates each case after seeing the outcome.
children: Comparing theories therefore requires attention to both fit and how much freedom produced it.

blocks.text: **The models compete over explanation, not over whether these basic reading patterns exist.** Shared behavioral success makes their differing assumptions especially important.
Agreement on the phenomena does not mean agreement on mechanisms. One account emphasizes specialized routes, while the other emphasizes learning across interacting representational systems.
**The same task pattern receives a different mechanistic explanation in each model.** Keep the observed phenomenon separate from the proposed locus of impairment.
For phonological dyslexia, DRC emphasizes GPC damage and the triangle account emphasizes broader phonological impairment.
children: For surface dyslexia, DRC emphasizes lexical-route damage and the triangle account emphasizes semantic impairment.

blocks.text: **Phonological and semantic measures can help identify what lies behind a reading dissociation.** They extend the evidence beyond the reading scores alone.
The statistical-learning account links phonology to spelling–sound generalization and semantics to words whose pronunciation is poorly supported by that generalization.
children: Both dissociations and associations matter. A theory should explain selective weaknesses and the related abilities that vary with them.

blocks.text: **Productive word formation goes beyond retrieving a stored list.** The theoretical issue is whether that productivity requires symbolic rules or can emerge from learning.
The central question is how a speaker extends a familiar pattern to a new item. English plural and past-tense formation provide tractable examples.
children: Generalization can also produce playful or incorrect forms. This shows productive use of patterns, rather than a vocabulary containing only previously heard responses.

blocks.text: **A novel item prevents success from being explained as retrieval of that item's memorized inflection.** The child must extend a learned pattern.
The pictured task introduces one WUG and then asks about two. Producing WUGS applies plural knowledge to a new noun.
children: The same logic can test past tense using novel verbs. Success shows productive knowledge, but does not by itself distinguish symbolic rules from statistical generalization.

blocks.text: **Past-tense knowledge includes generalization and item-specific variation.** The contrast creates a test for different theories of morphology.
Irregular pairs such as GO–WENT, TAKE–TOOK and EAT–ATE do not follow that default form. Some irregulars share smaller patterns with other verbs.
children: A theory must explain both familiar exceptions and productive extension to novel verbs.

blocks.text: **In this account, productive rule application and remembered exceptions are separate kinds of knowledge.** That is stronger than simply observing that regular and irregular forms look different.
The regular process can apply to a new verb because it does not require an entry for that particular past tense.
children: The irregular system stores word-specific information and can be influenced by frequency and similarity. A successful explanation also needs to prevent an available irregular form from being replaced by a regularization.

blocks.text: **Similar-looking architectures can solve different computational problems.** Keep morphological inflection separate from grapheme–phoneme conversion.
Pinker and Ullman's diagram associates lexical lookup with declarative memory and grammatical combination with procedural processing.
children: Like dual-route reading, the account separates word-specific knowledge from a productive operation. Unlike reading aloud, its task is to transform a stem according to a grammatical feature, rather than convert spelling into sound.

blocks.text: **The motivation for an architecture matters when evaluating its evidence.** Similar diagrams do not mean that the theories were derived from the same observations.

Reading dual-route theories were strongly motivated by neuropsychological dissociations. The morphology proposal also reflects a commitment to keeping the grammatical rule system distinct from exceptional lexical information.
**Separating exceptions protects a simple rule, but creates a second mechanism that must also be explained.** The associative system carries graded and item-specific influences.
KEEP–KEPT, WEEP–WEPT and LEAP–LEAPT illustrate similarity among irregular forms. An exception can belong to a small family rather than being wholly unrelated to other words.
children: Assigning these properties to lexical memory lets the rule system remain categorical and general.

blocks.text: **One learning mechanism is proposed for both regularities and exceptions.** The challenge is to explain accurate generalization as well as familiar forms.
The model encodes a root's phonology, transforms that representation through modifiable connections, and decodes an output pattern.
children: Regularity is a pattern learned from many examples. Irregular forms are also learned within the same system.

blocks.text: **Development can involve temporary errors as knowledge changes.** A theory must explain the entire trajectory, not just the final adult response.
The middle error is a **regularization**, because the child applies the common past-tense pattern to an irregular verb.
children: The decline does not necessarily mean that the child has stopped learning. A changing system can generalize more broadly while temporarily disrupting an earlier correct response.

blocks.text: **Overregularization is interpreted as productive rule use that is not yet sufficiently constrained by exceptions.** Recovery depends on the irregular form winning over the rule output.
When the rule is learned, it can be applied too broadly, yielding RUNNED. Later, learned irregulars and the blocking process prevent that regularization.
children: This account treats the developmental stages as involving distinguishable processes rather than only gradual changes in one mapping.

blocks.text: **A shift in the distribution of experience can temporarily disrupt familiar responses.** The learning account explains the developmental pattern through changing weights and input.
As more regular verbs enter training, their common pattern changes the network's responses. That generalization can interfere with previously learned irregulars.
children: With further learning, the network can recover the irregular responses while retaining broad regularity. No new symbolic rule component is inserted at the point of decline.

blocks.text: **Generalization is defined relative to the learner's experience.** A familiar human word is still a valid novel-model test when it was withheld from training.
The test therefore uses the logic of a wug task even when the items are real words to humans.
children: The model can generate many appropriate past-tense features, but feature-level success must be distinguished from producing an entirely correct word.

blocks.text: **A plausible learning curve is not enough if the model produces implausible words.** Error structure provides another test of the representation and decoding process.
The model authors acknowledge that people are unlikely to make some of these errors. They suggest that additional output constraints could reduce bizarre responses.
children: This separates capturing an overall learning pattern from matching the detailed form of human errors.

blocks.text: **Combining evidence for alternatives is different from blending the alternatives into a new malformed output.** A model must preserve the distinctions needed to produce a coherent response.
For SING, partial support for different sound patterns can overlap. Decoding the combined activation can produce a hybrid rather than selecting a coherent word.
children: The criticism targets the representation and its treatment of competing outputs, not merely the presence of learning.

blocks.text: **The regular–irregular contrast can arise from how phonological and semantic information contribute.** A graded system can produce systematic differences between item types.
Reliable sound representations support extension from familiar present–past pairs to new forms. Irregular mappings receive additional support from the particular word's semantic representation.
children: The hypothesis concerns different degrees of dependence on shared systems, rather than a separate symbolic rule route for every regular response.

blocks.text: **The same architecture should explain both sides of the patient pattern.** Selectivity must arise from the manipulated representations and their contribution to the task.
A nonword has no familiar item-specific semantic history to support its inflection. A known irregular can require semantic support because its output is not well predicted by the dominant pattern.
children: Manipulating phonological or semantic integrity tests whether these different dependencies can produce opposite impairment profiles.

blocks.text: **Difficulty with productive inflection may be connected to sound processing.** The nonword condition is particularly demanding because it relies on generalization.
Regular forms are also vulnerable, while irregular forms are relatively better in the displayed comparison. A novel BLICK must be transformed without relying on a familiar stored past tense.
children: This motivates investigating phonological contributions to the apparent morphological deficit.

blocks.text: **Damaging phonology can imitate a failure of productive morphology without removing a symbolic rule.** The mechanism being tested is the quality of sound representations.
The model manipulation weakens sound-based computation. Familiar words retain support unavailable to an untrained nonword.
children: The similarity to the patient pattern shows how a selective-looking morphological deficit can arise from a broader phonological impairment.

blocks.text: **Relatively preserved nonword inflection can coexist with poor irregular inflection.** The theory must explain this reverse pattern as well as phonological impairment.
Their irregular performance is lower than their regular and nonword performance in the displayed comparison.
children: This creates the other side of the dissociation and motivates examining the information that especially supports known irregular forms.

blocks.text: **Irregular vulnerability is predicted from its greater dependence on semantic support.** The model does not have to delete an isolated exception list to produce that pattern.
Typical phonological patterns still support many regular and novel forms. Nonwords can nevertheless be somewhat worse than regular words because they lack item-specific training.
children: This shows how unequal dependence on semantics can produce the reverse of the phonological-damage profile.

blocks.text: **A task dissociation should be checked for differences in the demands of its items.** Related abilities can explain why one condition is more vulnerable.
Patterson and colleagues found that irregular impairment in semantic dementia correlated with semantic deficit severity.
children: These findings connect morphology to phonological and semantic abilities, making a pure rule-versus-word interpretation less straightforward.

blocks.text: **Different forms draw on the same systems to different degrees.** General patterns and word-specific support can jointly determine an output.
Semantic information supports forms that depart from the dominant -ed pattern. Some irregulars also benefit from smaller phonological families and can be relatively spared.
children: Regularity and exception status therefore describe degrees of statistical support rather than perfectly isolated kinds of processing.

blocks.text: **The diagnostic description and the causal explanation are separate.** A grammatical difficulty can coexist with weaknesses in other processes that support language.
The profile can also involve phonology, reading, working memory and speech perception. This broader range matters when evaluating a theory that locates the problem only in grammar.
children: A relative language difficulty does not by itself identify a single damaged learning mechanism.

blocks.text: **The crucial issue is whether the deficit is selective enough to support the proposed rule mechanism.** Merely finding poor past tense does not establish its cause.
This proposal uses past-tense performance to argue for a mechanism specific to grammatical rules.
children: The prediction must be tested against the complete pattern, including irregular performance and broader phonological difficulties.

blocks.text: **The observed pattern is broader than a simple intact-irregulars versus damaged-rules contrast.** Novel forms are most vulnerable, while familiar forms are not unaffected.
Nonwords are especially difficult for the SLI group, but regulars and irregulars are also impaired. The results therefore contain a broad deficit as well as unequal condition difficulty.
children: An explanation should account for the entire profile rather than reporting only that productive forms are poor.

blocks.text: **A graded phonological manipulation creates graded developmental impairment.** Novel generalization is most fragile because it cannot rely on a word's own training history.
The intact model performs substantially better. Even intact learning shows different performance across regulars, irregulars and nonwords.
children: The comparison tests whether a phonological learning weakness can reproduce important aspects of the behavioral profile without a missing grammatical rule.

blocks.text: **An especially large nonword deficit does not imply that other forms avoid phonology.** It reflects different degrees of dependence on generalization.
Nonwords are particularly dependent on generalizing a sound pattern to a new form. Familiar words have additional item-specific learning that can partly support their responses.

**Past-tense behavior can be explained through learned structure and unequal support from shared representations.** The proposal must still explain developmental, patient and generalization data together.
Irregular performance is associated with semantic processing. Wug-test performance is associated with phonological processing.
children: These associations provide tests of the proposed underlying mechanisms, beyond simply assigning different item types to different boxes.

blocks.text: **Influencing thought is different from completely determining thought.** Keep that distinction explicit when interpreting a language-group difference.
The strongest reading would make language determine what a person can think. A weaker claim is that habitual language use biases attention, memory or preferred ways of representing a situation.
children: These claims require different evidence. A preference associated with language does not establish that alternative thought is impossible.

blocks.text: **Testing linguistic relativity requires a narrower claim than saying that every language creates a completely separate world.** Space and time provide specific domains in which to test representational preferences.
Sapir and Whorf should not automatically be assigned the strongest deterministic interpretation of selected quotations.
children: A precise study must identify which cognitive process is affected and what alternative explanations the comparison controls.

blocks.text: **The object does not have to move for its verbal description to change.** Changing the reference frame changes the relation being described.
The ball can be located with respect to the viewer, the chair's own orientation or a direction independent of either.
children: Different descriptions can identify the same physical position while organizing that position differently.

blocks.text: **Ask what fixes the direction in each description.** The object's orientation, the observer's body and a stable external direction are not interchangeable.
“At the chair's front” uses the chair's intrinsic front. “To the left of the chair from my viewpoint” depends on the observer.
children: “North of the chair” uses an absolute direction that does not reverse when the observer turns around.

blocks.text: **A direction can stay fixed when a person turns.** Absolute coding differs from coding an object as being on the viewer's left.
Tzeltal commonly uses absolute directions in circumstances where English speakers might use these relative terms.
children: The contrast motivates asking whether habitual language use relates to nonverbal spatial coding, rather than merely comparing two ways of giving spoken directions.

blocks.text: **A landmark origin and an absolute use are different properties.** A historically landscape-based term can become a stable directional reference.
A direction is retained as a stable spatial reference rather than being recalculated from the speaker's current left and right.
children: This allows positions to be described consistently as the speaker changes orientation.

blocks.text: **A stable local convention is not automatically an absolute frame that transfers everywhere.** Its usefulness depends on the landmark system being available.
A city's conventional map orientation can also differ from magnetic north. Familiar spatial language therefore reflects local practices as well as geometric directions.
**The rotation makes two otherwise similar descriptions predict different choices.** The nonverbal response reveals a preferred spatial coding strategy.
A relative response preserves the arrangement with respect to the person's viewpoint. An absolute response preserves its orientation in the environment, so the two responses diverge after rotation.
children: Dutch speakers predominantly gave relative responses, while Tzeltal speakers gave more absolute responses. The association is consistent with their preferred linguistic frames but does not isolate language from all other experience.

blocks.text: **The task goes beyond reproducing one remembered arrangement.** It asks whether a frame is used when combining spatial relations to make an inference.
They then place an object relative to another using the combined information. Relative and absolute coding lead to different placements because the person's orientation has changed.
children: Dutch and Tzeltal response patterns again differ in the direction associated with their preferred spatial frames.

blocks.text: **A language comparison can be confounded with a setting comparison.** The environment must be considered before assigning the entire difference to linguistic structure.
An environment with useful landmarks can encourage landmark-based coding. A windowless laboratory can make viewer-relative descriptions more convenient.
children: Manipulating landmark availability within English speakers tests whether the behavior can change without changing native language.

blocks.text: **Spatial strategy is sensitive to the testing environment.** A within-language change helps reveal a potential confound in a between-language comparison.
The manipulation changes the spatial information available while keeping the language group the same.
children: This demonstrates that task context can influence the response. It challenges an explanation in which language alone fixes the chosen frame.

blocks.text: **The relevant question is what the study actually isolates.** A language-group effect can be real while its causal interpretation remains unsettled.
A controlled comparison must separate the effect of the environment from any contribution of habitual linguistic coding.
children: Showing an environmental effect does not prove that language never matters. It limits what can be inferred from an uncontrolled comparison.

blocks.text: **Changing a task can change the process it measures.** A landmark effect in an easy, transparent task may not settle how people habitually remember spatial relations.
Participants who infer what is being tested can alter their response for reasons different from habitual spatial coding.
children: The response therefore focuses on memory load and task transparency, rather than denying that landmarks can ever matter.

blocks.text: **A relative preference can persist despite changes in the environment when the memory task is more demanding.** This narrows the conditions under which the landmark alternative explains behavior.
Under these conditions, the preference for relative coding remained.
children: The result suggests that the environmental effect depends on how the task is arranged, including how much memory and strategic inference it encourages.

blocks.text: **The involvement of memory creates another mechanism to examine.** A task can be nonverbal in its response while still allowing verbal recoding internally.
The relative preference is reported when memory demands are substantial and the experimenter's interest is less obvious.
children: That pattern makes it important to ask how the sequence is stored during the delay, not only which direction is chosen at the end.

blocks.text: **A nonverbal task does not guarantee nonverbal processing.** Verbal recoding is a concrete alternative mechanism for the spatial-memory result.
This strategy would connect language to the task through working memory and ordering habits, rather than through an inability to represent absolute space.
children: The interpretation changes because the same choice can arise from different internal codes.

blocks.text: **An expression can be meaningful without being literal.** The study of time asks whether familiar spatial expressions also relate to cognitive processing.
Physical and spatial terms can therefore help express abstract relations. Time is especially useful for studying whether such linguistic habits are associated with nonlinguistic representations.
children: The question is empirical. Using a spatial phrase does not by itself prove that every thought about time has the same spatial format.

blocks.text: **Habitual ways of talking about time can suggest testable predictions about processing.** Mandarin's vertical terms make a vertical temporal organization a relevant possibility.
The linguistic contrast motivates testing whether speakers differ in the spatial organization they use during temporal tasks.
children: The existence of the expressions is the starting observation. A behavioral task is needed to investigate whether the contrast extends beyond words.

blocks.text: **The prime changes what representation is active before the temporal judgment.** Response-time differences reveal compatibility between the prime and the later task.
English speakers respond faster after horizontal than vertical primes, while Mandarin speakers show the opposite pattern in the displayed comparison.
children: Training English speakers on vertical metaphors changes the pattern toward a vertical-prime advantage. This suggests sensitivity to experience, rather than an unchangeable division between language groups.

blocks.text: **Language-group differences can bundle linguistic and literacy experiences together.** Reading direction therefore needs to be measured or controlled.
Casasanto and Bottini use differences in text orientation and arrangement preferences to motivate this alternative.
children: The point is to identify another source of spatial experience, not to assume that a writing-system label perfectly predicts every individual's habits.

blocks.text: **A targeted control tests a specific alternative explanation.** Its conclusion should be limited to the experience that was actually controlled.
English speakers show an advantage for a left-is-earlier horizontal mapping. Mandarin speakers also show an advantage for a top-is-earlier vertical mapping in the displayed comparison.
children: Retaining a vertical effect under this restriction weakens that particular reading-direction explanation, without proving that every possible experiential confound is removed.

blocks.text: **Changing which side corresponds to past allows a direct test of spatial–temporal compatibility.** Color alone cannot explain the pattern because the mappings are counterbalanced.
With standard text reading, responses are faster when past maps left and future maps right.
children: Because the response concerns time rather than an explicit judgment of spatial direction, the compatibility effect reveals an implicit spatial association in this task.

blocks.text: **A flexible temporal mapping is difficult to explain as a fixed consequence of native-language grammar alone.** Recent perceptual and reading experience contributes to performance.
By the second mirror-reading block, the compatibility effect reverses. Responses are faster when earlier maps right and later maps left.
children: The result supports a contribution of reading-direction experience and shows that the association can change over a short period.

blocks.text: **Different lexical packaging does not show that one group cannot understand another group's distinctions.** The linguistic facts and the cognitive inference both need scrutiny.
Languages can express distinctions through separate roots, derived words or phrases. Counting one of these forms without considering the others can misrepresent expressive capacity.
children: A reliable claim requires accurate linguistic description and an appropriate behavioral test, rather than repetition of a striking anecdote.

blocks.text: **Do not treat Braille as a signed language or signing as a tactile alphabet.** They provide different tests of language and neural plasticity.
The distinction matters because changing the modality of a language is not the same as changing how a written language is accessed.
children: Both cases reveal how sensory experience shapes the organization of systems involved in language and reading.

blocks.text: **Changing the articulators does not remove linguistic organization.** Signed languages remain structured systems rather than collections of transparent gestures.
Space can carry linguistic relations. Some signs are iconic, meaning that aspects of their form resemble aspects of their meaning.
children: Iconicity is easy to overestimate when a familiar translation is supplied. A visible resemblance does not eliminate the need to learn a language's forms and structure.

blocks.text: **The unit of analysis is coordinated language production, not an isolated hand pose.** Fluency depends on how the articulators work together.
Like speech, a fluent stream is continuous enough that word boundaries are not always obvious to a learner.
children: Eye contact and movement timing are therefore relevant to perceiving the interaction, alongside the form of individual signs.

blocks.text: **A feature is linguistically contrastive when changing it changes the sign identity.** Visual similarity alone does not determine whether two forms belong to the same category.
The PLEASE–SORRY and ONION–APPLE examples demonstrate that closely related visible forms can have different linguistic identities.
children: Phonology therefore concerns the organization of contrastive form, not only acoustic sound.

blocks.text: **The test distinguishes a physical change from a linguistically meaningful category change.** Both continua vary visually, but only one crosses the relevant contrast.
One continuum crosses a phonemic distinction between PLEASE and SORRY. The allophonic comparison varies hand configuration without the same change in sign identity.
children: A sharp identification boundary accompanied by better discrimination near that boundary would indicate category-sensitive perception.

blocks.text: **The combination of a sharp identification shift and a boundary-related discrimination peak supports categorical perception.** Identification alone would provide a less complete test.
Discrimination is also strongest near the phonemic boundary. Comparable physical steps are easier to distinguish when they cross that category boundary.
children: The allophonic identification function is shallower and lacks the same localized discrimination peak. This links the perceptual pattern to linguistic contrast rather than any visible hand change.

blocks.text: **Where a sign is made can be part of the sentence's meaning.** The listener must track linguistic relations across space as well as over time.
Understanding a sentence can require retaining where entities were introduced and how subsequent signs relate to those locations.
children: Spatial processing therefore contributes to linguistic comprehension, rather than functioning only as background vision.

blocks.text: **Different sensory inputs can engage overlapping language networks.** The additional visual and spatial activity reflects the demands of processing a signed signal.
Signing also engages visual and superior parietal regions relevant to its perceptual and spatial demands.
children: The combination suggests both common language organization and modality-related contributions. Similarity does not require identical activation everywhere.

blocks.text: **The comparison groups are essential to the causal question.** A deaf-versus-hearing contrast alone would bundle deafness and signing experience together.
Deaf participants showed an advantage when attention was directed to the periphery.
children: Including hearing signers helps separate experience with signing from lack of auditory input. If all signers had the same advantage, signing alone would be a stronger explanation.

blocks.text: **Do not combine lateralization and peripheral attention into one undifferentiated advantage.** They track different aspects of experience.
Enhanced peripheral attention is found in deaf individuals, not hearing signers. Signing experience alone therefore does not explain that enhancement.
children: The proposed interpretations involve links between motion and language systems for signing, and reduced reliance on auditory peripheral cues in deafness.

blocks.text: **A useful control shares some demands while differing in the process being tested.** Tic-tac helps separate language comprehension from hand-motion processing.
Both tasks involve meaningful, sequenced hand movements. A difference between them is more informative about linguistic processing than a comparison between signing and no movement.
children: The control is not identical to a natural language, which is precisely why the remaining difference is of interest.

blocks.text: **Shared visual movement does not explain the entire neural response to signed language.** The temporal-region difference is the central language-related result.
The comparison reduces a simple explanation based only on the presence of hands moving through space.
children: The frontal activation shown is superior to classic Broca's area, so it should not be casually relabeled as a precise Broca's effect.

blocks.text: **A coherent account must separate shared language organization from sensory adaptations.** Neither “sign is just gesture” nor “modality makes no difference” captures the evidence.
Signing experience is associated with changes in motion lateralization. Deafness is associated with enhanced peripheral attention in the reported comparison.
children: These findings jointly show that linguistic experience and sensory history contribute in different ways.

blocks.text: **Spatial comprehension depends on conventions as well as geometric convenience.** The observer may transform a speaker-centered description rather than prefer an already reversed one.
The figure's caption reports better comprehension for descriptions from the speaker's perspective despite the mental transformation that this requires.
children: This illustrates that the most linguistically natural representation is not necessarily the one that eliminates every spatial transformation.

blocks.text: **The linguistic task can remain reading while the sensory input changes.** This makes Braille useful for studying cross-modal organization.
The symbols are optimized for touch. Fingers acquire letters sequentially, creating perceptual demands that differ from viewing printed text.
children: The comparison asks how reading networks operate when the input arrives through touch instead of vision.

blocks.text: **The timing of sensory experience relates to later functional organization.** Visual cortex can participate in tactile reading even when the stimulus is not visual.
Early-blind participants show stronger involvement of regions associated with visual word processing than late-blind participants.
children: This indicates that a region's usual sensory label does not completely determine the information it can help process.

blocks.text: **Cross-modal changes do not have to be limited to early development.** A short-term manipulation can reveal latent contributions to tactile processing.
The blindfolded group learned more quickly. This suggests that eliminating competing visual input can affect tactile learning over a short timescale.
children: Because the participants were sighted adults, the experiment tests a different question from lifelong or early blindness.

blocks.text: **Reversibility helps constrain the mechanism.** A rapid response that disappears after vision returns suggests a change in functional contribution or competition.
Removing visual input can allow tactile-related activity to become more evident. Restoring vision changes that balance again.
children: This pattern is consistent with unmasking existing inputs rather than requiring the creation of an entirely new pathway over a few days.

blocks.text: **Activation and necessity are different kinds of evidence.** Interfering with a region and changing behavior provides stronger evidence that its activity contributes to the task.
On Day 5, the blindfolded group's error rate rises under 1 Hz TMS relative to its baseline and sham conditions. The nonblindfolded group does not show the same selective disruption.
children: The effect is no longer present in the same way after blindfold removal. The result supports a temporary functional contribution of visual cortex to tactile performance.

blocks.text: **A brain region's contribution reflects development and competition as well as its usual sensory input.** Common language functions can coexist with modality-specific adaptations.
Competition among available inputs offers a way to understand reorganization. When an input is absent or reduced, other information can make a larger contribution.
children: The evidence does not imply that all regions are interchangeable. It shows both stable functional relationships and experience-sensitive recruitment.

blocks.text: **An unfamiliar spelling cannot always be decoded correctly from its letters alone.** Deep orthographies create more exceptions that readers must learn through experience.
COLONEL and PARADIGM make the problem concrete. Applying common letter–sound patterns can produce a plausible-looking pronunciation that is wrong for the actual word.
children: In shallower writing systems, such as Finnish and Korean, spelling–sound correspondences are more predictable. The comparison concerns the writing system, not the intelligence or ability of its readers.

blocks.text: **Consistent correspondences make decoding easier to generalize.** Finnish readers can apply what they learn about letters to unfamiliar written forms.
Doubled letters represent a meaningful length distinction. A doubled consonant is geminated, and a doubled vowel is long.
children: This regularity helps Finnish children learn decoding quickly. Decoding means generating a pronunciation from a written form, whether or not its meaning is familiar.

blocks.text: **A made-up word separates decoding from remembering a familiar word.** The lower English performance is consistent with greater orthographic depth.

The comparison involves Grade 1 children learning different alphabetic writing systems. Children learning many other languages produce plausible pseudoword pronunciations more successfully than English learners.
children: English's less predictable correspondences help explain why decoding develops more slowly. This task does not measure the child's entire language ability.

blocks.text: **The organization of Hangul supports more than consistent pronunciation.** Similar sound categories can also be visibly related in their written symbols.
The letters are arranged into syllable blocks with initial, medial and sometimes final positions. Those positions are not three unrelated pictures of whole words.
children: The velar consonant forms share the basic angular ㄱ shape. Additional strokes or doubling distinguish related consonants.

blocks.text: **Experience matters especially when pronunciation conflicts with the usual spelling pattern.** Frequent exposure reduces the disadvantage of exception words.
Naming latency is the time needed to begin saying the word. Higher values mean slower responses.
children: An interaction means the effect of one factor depends on the other. The regularity cost is not a fixed amount added equally to high- and low-frequency words.

blocks.text: **Two routes can explain why regularity matters most for unfamiliar words.** Fast lexical processing protects familiar exceptions from competing sublexical output.
For a high-frequency word, lexical information becomes available quickly enough to reduce the influence of the decoding output.
children: For a low-frequency exception, the lexical response is less efficient and the regularized decoding output can interfere. Nonwords depend on decoding because they lack a stored whole-word entry.

blocks.text: **Word-specific knowledge and generalization can coexist in the same learned system.** They do not have to be implemented as a dictionary and a separate symbolic rule list.
The same learning mechanism can capture both patterns shared by many words and information specific to a familiar word.
children: The research strategy asks whether domain-general learning can explain reading. This contrasts with choosing separate adult processing components primarily from neuropsychological dissociations.

blocks.text: **Consistency supplies support from other words, while frequency strengthens experience with the particular word.** Their joint influence explains why infrequent exceptions are especially difficult.
An exception conflicts with those patterns, so learning its particular mapping is especially important. Frequent exposure strengthens that word-specific mapping.
children: A low-frequency exception has both weak item-specific learning and poor support from the dominant pattern. This combination creates a larger disadvantage than either factor alone.

blocks.text: **Novel pronunciation can result from applying learned statistical structure.** Nonword reading therefore does not automatically establish a separate symbolic route.
No stored entry for the particular nonword is required. The same learned correspondences that support consistent words can support a new combination.
children: This is a proposed mechanism for decoding without a separate GPC rule module.

blocks.text: **A failed simulation does not identify its own cause.** The failure must be traced to the architecture, learning assumptions, representations or other implementation choices.
One possibility is that a single associative mechanism cannot explain the task. Another is that the chosen representations fail to capture the similarities needed for generalization.
children: Improving the implementation while retaining the theoretical mechanism helps distinguish these possibilities.

blocks.text: **Changing the representation can improve decoding without adding a symbolic rule system.** That distinction matters when evaluating the original theoretical claim.
Plaut and colleagues improved the phonological representations and obtained better nonword performance. This supports a representational explanation for at least part of the earlier failure.
children: Behavioral relations between phonological processing and decoding also make phonology a relevant target for explanation.

blocks.text: **The same representational weakness can have unequal effects on words and nonwords.** Familiarity can partly compensate where new-item generalization cannot.
A familiar word can retain support from its own training history. A nonword lacks that item-specific experience and depends more heavily on generalization.
children: This produces a reason for unfamiliar forms to be especially vulnerable to poor representations without requiring a dedicated nonword mechanism.

blocks.text: **A selective-looking reading deficit can emerge from degraded shared representations.** Nonwords are especially dependent on reliable generalization.
The manipulation produced poorer nonword decoding and relative sparing of word recognition. It also linked the severity of the phonological deficit to the degree of decoding difficulty.
children: The model therefore connects a reading pattern to the quality of a more general phonological system.

blocks.text: **Similar-looking architectures can solve different computational problems.** Keep morphological inflection separate from grapheme–phoneme conversion.
Pinker and Ullman's diagram associates lexical lookup with declarative memory and grammatical combination with procedural processing.
children: Like dual-route reading, the account separates word-specific knowledge from a productive operation. Unlike reading aloud, its task is to transform a stem according to a grammatical feature, rather than convert spelling into sound.

blocks.text: **The motivation for an architecture matters when evaluating its evidence.** Similar diagrams do not mean that the theories were derived from the same observations.

Reading dual-route theories were strongly motivated by neuropsychological dissociations. The morphology proposal also reflects a commitment to keeping the grammatical rule system distinct from exceptional lexical information.
**Separating exceptions protects a simple rule, but creates a second mechanism that must also be explained.** The associative system carries graded and item-specific influences.
KEEP–KEPT, WEEP–WEPT and LEAP–LEAPT illustrate similarity among irregular forms. An exception can belong to a small family rather than being wholly unrelated to other words.
children: Assigning these properties to lexical memory lets the rule system remain categorical and general.

blocks.text: **One learning mechanism is proposed for both regularities and exceptions.** The challenge is to explain accurate generalization as well as familiar forms.
The model encodes a root's phonology, transforms that representation through modifiable connections, and decodes an output pattern.
children: Regularity is a pattern learned from many examples. Irregular forms are also learned within the same system.

blocks.text: **Development can involve temporary errors as knowledge changes.** A theory must explain the entire trajectory, not just the final adult response.
The middle error is a **regularization**, because the child applies the common past-tense pattern to an irregular verb.
children: The decline does not necessarily mean that the child has stopped learning. A changing system can generalize more broadly while temporarily disrupting an earlier correct response.

blocks.text: **Overregularization is interpreted as productive rule use that is not yet sufficiently constrained by exceptions.** Recovery depends on the irregular form winning over the rule output.
When the rule is learned, it can be applied too broadly, yielding RUNNED. Later, learned irregulars and the blocking process prevent that regularization.
children: This account treats the developmental stages as involving distinguishable processes rather than only gradual changes in one mapping.

blocks.text: **A shift in the distribution of experience can temporarily disrupt familiar responses.** The learning account explains the developmental pattern through changing weights and input.
As more regular verbs enter training, their common pattern changes the network's responses. That generalization can interfere with previously learned irregulars.
children: With further learning, the network can recover the irregular responses while retaining broad regularity. No new symbolic rule component is inserted at the point of decline.

blocks.text: **Generalization is defined relative to the learner's experience.** A familiar human word is still a valid novel-model test when it was withheld from training.
The test therefore uses the logic of a wug task even when the items are real words to humans.
children: The model can generate many appropriate past-tense features, but feature-level success must be distinguished from producing an entirely correct word.

blocks.text: **A plausible learning curve is not enough if the model produces implausible words.** Error structure provides another test of the representation and decoding process.
The model authors acknowledge that people are unlikely to make some of these errors. They suggest that additional output constraints could reduce bizarre responses.
children: This separates capturing an overall learning pattern from matching the detailed form of human errors.

blocks.text: **The regular–irregular contrast can arise from how phonological and semantic information contribute.** A graded system can produce systematic differences between item types.
Reliable sound representations support extension from familiar present–past pairs to new forms. Irregular mappings receive additional support from the particular word's semantic representation.
children: The hypothesis concerns different degrees of dependence on shared systems, rather than a separate symbolic rule route for every regular response.

blocks.text: **The same architecture should explain both sides of the patient pattern.** Selectivity must arise from the manipulated representations and their contribution to the task.
A nonword has no familiar item-specific semantic history to support its inflection. A known irregular can require semantic support because its output is not well predicted by the dominant pattern.
children: Manipulating phonological or semantic integrity tests whether these different dependencies can produce opposite impairment profiles.

blocks.text: **Difficulty with productive inflection may be connected to sound processing.** The nonword condition is particularly demanding because it relies on generalization.
Regular forms are also vulnerable, while irregular forms are relatively better in the displayed comparison. A novel BLICK must be transformed without relying on a familiar stored past tense.
children: This motivates investigating phonological contributions to the apparent morphological deficit.

blocks.text: **Relatively preserved nonword inflection can coexist with poor irregular inflection.** The theory must explain this reverse pattern as well as phonological impairment.
Their irregular performance is lower than their regular and nonword performance in the displayed comparison.
children: This creates the other side of the dissociation and motivates examining the information that especially supports known irregular forms.

blocks.text: **Fluency, grammatical organization and meaningful word selection are distinguishable dimensions.** The two example profiles emphasize different disruptions.
This makes a lexical-versus-grammatical interpretation attractive. However, a descriptive syndrome is not itself a demonstration of an isolated processing module.
children: Content words may be relatively preserved in telegraphic speech, while fluent speech can retain sentence-like structure without conveying a clear message.

blocks.text: **A familiar syndrome name does not settle which level of processing is affected.** Articulation and grammatical formulation must be distinguished.
**Apraxia of speech** concerns planning or coordinating speech movements. That differs from explaining an omission of grammatical structure in otherwise producible speech.
children: The historical label therefore should not substitute for a precise description of the impaired behavior.

blocks.text: **Syntax and meaning can come apart in a judgment without proving a perfectly modular neural organization.** The behavioral and theoretical claims should be kept separate.
Chomsky's example of a grammatical but semantically unusual sentence shows that syntactic well-formedness cannot be reduced to whether a sentence describes a sensible event.
children: That conceptual distinction does not establish a simple one-to-one mapping from each syndrome to one isolated component.

blocks.text: **Word selection, ordering, sound encoding and articulation are different explanatory levels.** An apparent lexical–grammatical contrast should be related to those operations carefully.
A **lemma** is a representation involved in lexical selection, distinct from simply executing its sound pattern. Positional processing contributes ordering and morphological structure.
children: Combinations such as HOUSEBOAT show that complex-word meaning can be partly compositional. Errors such as “easy enoughly” provide evidence about the organization of morphological operations.

blocks.text: **A direction can stay fixed when a person turns.** Absolute coding differs from coding an object as being on the viewer's left.
Tzeltal commonly uses absolute directions in circumstances where English speakers might use these relative terms.
children: The contrast motivates asking whether habitual language use relates to nonverbal spatial coding, rather than merely comparing two ways of giving spoken directions.

blocks.text: **A landmark origin and an absolute use are different properties.** A historically landscape-based term can become a stable directional reference.
A direction is retained as a stable spatial reference rather than being recalculated from the speaker's current left and right.
children: This allows positions to be described consistently as the speaker changes orientation.

blocks.text: **The rotation makes two otherwise similar descriptions predict different choices.** The nonverbal response reveals a preferred spatial coding strategy.
A relative response preserves the arrangement with respect to the person's viewpoint. An absolute response preserves its orientation in the environment, so the two responses diverge after rotation.
children: Dutch speakers predominantly gave relative responses, while Tzeltal speakers gave more absolute responses. The association is consistent with their preferred linguistic frames but does not isolate language from all other experience.

blocks.text: **The task goes beyond reproducing one remembered arrangement.** It asks whether a frame is used when combining spatial relations to make an inference.
They then place an object relative to another using the combined information. Relative and absolute coding lead to different placements because the person's orientation has changed.
children: Dutch and Tzeltal response patterns again differ in the direction associated with their preferred spatial frames.

blocks.text: **A language comparison can be confounded with a setting comparison.** The environment must be considered before assigning the entire difference to linguistic structure.
An environment with useful landmarks can encourage landmark-based coding. A windowless laboratory can make viewer-relative descriptions more convenient.
children: Manipulating landmark availability within English speakers tests whether the behavior can change without changing native language.

blocks.text: **Spatial strategy is sensitive to the testing environment.** A within-language change helps reveal a potential confound in a between-language comparison.
The manipulation changes the spatial information available while keeping the language group the same.
children: This demonstrates that task context can influence the response. It challenges an explanation in which language alone fixes the chosen frame.

blocks.text: **Changing a task can change the process it measures.** A landmark effect in an easy, transparent task may not settle how people habitually remember spatial relations.
Participants who infer what is being tested can alter their response for reasons different from habitual spatial coding.
children: The response therefore focuses on memory load and task transparency, rather than denying that landmarks can ever matter.

blocks.text: **The test distinguishes a physical change from a linguistically meaningful category change.** Both continua vary visually, but only one crosses the relevant contrast.
One continuum crosses a phonemic distinction between PLEASE and SORRY. The allophonic comparison varies hand configuration without the same change in sign identity.
children: A sharp identification boundary accompanied by better discrimination near that boundary would indicate category-sensitive perception.

blocks.text: **The combination of a sharp identification shift and a boundary-related discrimination peak supports categorical perception.** Identification alone would provide a less complete test.
Discrimination is also strongest near the phonemic boundary. Comparable physical steps are easier to distinguish when they cross that category boundary.
children: The allophonic identification function is shallower and lacks the same localized discrimination peak. This links the perceptual pattern to linguistic contrast rather than any visible hand change.

blocks.text: **Different sensory inputs can engage overlapping language networks.** The additional visual and spatial activity reflects the demands of processing a signed signal.
Signing also engages visual and superior parietal regions relevant to its perceptual and spatial demands.
children: The combination suggests both common language organization and modality-related contributions. Similarity does not require identical activation everywhere.

blocks.text: **A coherent account must separate shared language organization from sensory adaptations.** Neither “sign is just gesture” nor “modality makes no difference” captures the evidence.
Signing experience is associated with changes in motion lateralization. Deafness is associated with enhanced peripheral attention in the reported comparison.
children: These findings jointly show that linguistic experience and sensory history contribute in different ways.

blocks.text: **A late L2 learner has already exercised language capacity.** That history is what makes late-L2 outcomes informative for distinguishing the two proposals.
Later second-language difficulty in people who already acquired a first language is more directly compatible with maturation than with complete preservation through exercise.
children: This does not make early first-language experience unimportant. Early access and age-related change address related but distinct questions.

blocks.text: **Age of starting ASL is not the same as age of first language access.** Earlier linguistic experience can support learning a new language later.

Children first exposed to ASL at ages 9–15 had particular difficulty when it was also their first language. Those who had first learned a spoken language did much better, and the differences persisted.
children: The comparison distinguishes late first-language learning from late acquisition of an additional language.

blocks.text: **A control is informative when it tests the alternative mechanism directly.** Matching appearance and manipulating visual similarity provide complementary evidence.
The materials were normed so that same-category items were not more visually similar on average. A separate visual-similarity manipulation also produced a different time course.
children: Visual blocking affected the first block, whereas the semantic pattern of interest developed differently. This weakens a purely visual explanation.

blocks.text: **Separating display timing from naming order helps locate the source of interference.** Simultaneous visibility does not remove the need for sequential lexical selection.
Displaying all objects at once reduces dependence on a succession of isolated pictures. Serial naming still requires selecting and producing one label after another.
children: Eye tracking provides additional timing information about the processing of each object.

blocks.text: **One total naming time can conceal several processes.** Coordinating eye and speech measures reveals where a condition begins to change performance.
A participant can move the eyes toward the next object before articulating the current one. The measures therefore separate overlapping parts of preparation.
children: Different blocking effects on these measures can help constrain the processing stage affected.

blocks.text: **The location of the effect across measures matters more than a general statement that naming is slower.** Its time course and selectivity constrain the proposed mechanism.
Speech duration decreases with repetition without a blocking difference. Gaze duration shows the condition difference after the first cycle.
children: The nonsignificant lag difference should not be reported as evidence for a reversed effect. The reported pattern is interpreted as supporting a contribution at lemma selection rather than articulation or phonological encoding.

blocks.text: **The critical test is whether within-category differences influence lexical responses.** A binary final choice alone may hide that information.
**Voice onset time**, or VOT, varies the timing between release and voicing. It can change how strongly the sound supports /b/ or /p/.
children: A thresholded account would pass a completed categorical decision onward. A cascaded account allows graded information to influence word candidates before uncertainty is fully resolved.

blocks.text: **A forced choice can end in one category even when processing used graded evidence.** Eye movements provide a separate measure of that processing.
Shorter VOTs favored the /b/ response and longer VOTs the /p/ response. Near the boundary, the preferred category changed rapidly.
children: A categorical-looking final response does not establish that all earlier lexical activation was categorical.

blocks.text: **Final identification and moment-by-moment competition reveal different aspects of processing.** A sharp choice boundary can coexist with graded lexical uncertainty.
A participant can ultimately select BEAR while spending more time looking at PEAR when the sound is close to the boundary.
children: This supports the claim that fine phonetic information remains relevant to lexical activation, rather than disappearing completely after a categorical phoneme decision.

blocks.text: **The relevant predictor is distance from the boundary, not only which side of it the token occupies.** Similar final choices can still have different lexical-competition profiles.
The graph separates early and late observation windows. The gradient remains visible in the later competition measure, supporting continued sensitivity to within-category phonetic detail.
children: The result favors cascaded use of graded evidence over a model that transmits only a completed phoneme label with all within-category detail discarded.
